chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Muhammad al-Wabishi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a group that claimed a crime upon a slave, the damage of which exceeded his value, so the slave confessed to it. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The confession of the slave upon his master is not valid. So if they establish proof upon what they claimed against the slave, the slave is taken for it, or his master ransoms him.'

key_terms.يَفْتَدِيهِ: Ransoms him (pays compensation on his behalf)
key_terms.يُحِيطُ بِرَقَبَتِهِ: Exceeds the value of the slave's neck (self)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a slave's confession for a crime exceeding his value?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of individual liability in *diyah* (blood money), ruling that a slave’s confession does not automatically impose the debt on his master unless the master chooses to ransom him. This highlights the distinct legal personality of the slave in Shia jurisprudence, where the master is not strictly liable for the slave's personal crimes unless he assumes the cost, reflecting the balance between ownership rights and individual accountability.
